ta-l1d38q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 38. Having shown what God's knowledge is of, Lombard treats it in relation to the things known: whether it causes them, and then (Dist. 39) what kind of cause it is. He shows by reason and authority that God's knowledge is the cause of things, then that it is neither their cause nor caused by them (otherwise it would cause all evils), and cites Origen that something will not happen because God knows it will; he resolves this by saying future things are in no way the cause of foreknowledge. He then addresses the ineffability of God's knowledge, answering an objection and a renewed objection. Five articles are announced: whether God's knowledge causes things; whether he knows all uniformly; whether it is of enuntiables; whether of non-beings; and whether of contingents.
claims: God's knowledge is not caused by things; future things do not cause foreknowledge.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e128.summary: First argument that God's knowledge causes things. Saints and prophets compare it to an artisan's knowledge, which causes what is produced by art.
claims: God's knowledge is like an artisan's.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e131.summary: Second argument. Likeness is unity in form, so in every assimilation either one causes the other or both come from one cause. Knowledge is assimilation, so either knowledge causes the known (practical), the known causes knowledge (our speculative), or both have one cause (angelic knowledge, species impressed by God in the angel's mind and in matter). Nothing causes God's knowledge, so it causes the known.
claims: Assimilation requires a causal relation.
concepts: three relations of knowledge and thing

ta-l1d38q1-d1e134.summary: Third argument. A measure is principle of the measured (Metaphysics 10), and God's knowledge measures things, each having truth when it fulfils what it is ordered to in the divine mind (Anselm).
claims: God's knowledge measures things.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e138.summary: Fourth argument. As God's will is God, so is his knowledge, and his will is called absolutely the cause of all willed and his goodness of all goods.
claims: Will is called cause of things.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e141.summary: Sed contra. Whatever God's knowledge causes, God causes, but God does not cause all he knows, since evils, which he knows, are not from him.
claims: God does not cause evils.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e144.summary: Second sed contra. Given the cause, the effect follows, and God's knowledge was eternal but things were not.
claims: An eternal cause would yield eternal effects.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e147.summary: Thomas's determination. With divine attributes we must attend to their concepts, which differ, so something is attributed to one and not another though all are one thing: divine goodness causes goods, life the living. Some attributes relate not only to their possessor but to an object (power, will, knowledge), others only to the possessor (life, goodness). All have one mode of causality, as common efficient exemplar (from the first good all goods, from the first living all living), but those with objects have another causality toward their objects, as will toward the willed, and the question is about this for knowledge. God's knowledge is clearly the efficient and exemplar cause of all knowledges, but is it the cause of things known? Knowledge as such implies no causality, or all knowledge would cause, but an operating artisan's knowledge causes what art makes, so divine knowledge's causality should be considered like the artisan's. In producing an artefact, art shows the end, the will intends it, the will commands the act that brings out the work, and on the work the artisan's knowledge places the conceived form; so knowledge shows the end and the form, and will directs the act and informs the work. So whatever happens in the effect by defect from the art-form or the end does not reduce to the artisan's knowledge as cause, and the principal causality lies with the will that commands the act. So evil, deviation from form and end, is not caused by God's knowledge, which causes only goods insofar as they follow the form and end of divine art, and even these not with complete causality unless joined to will, which is why the text calls the knowledge of approval (beneplaciti) the cause of things, and Avicenna says things flow from God as he knows and loves or wills his essence as principle of the things he wills to be principle of.
claims: God's knowledge causes things as an artisan's art, showing end and form, but complete causality requires will.
God's knowledge does not cause evils, which deviate from form and end.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e150.summary: Reply to the first argument. An artisan's knowledge does not cause defects in the artefact, though foreseen, nor is it a complete cause without will (Metaphysics 9), and so with God's knowledge.
claims: Knowledge needs will to cause completely.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e153.summary: Reply to the second argument. God knows evils not by his likeness but by the likeness of goods (Dist. 36), so his knowledge causes only goods.
claims: Evils are known through goods, not caused.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e157.summary: Reply to the third argument. God's knowledge is called the measure of things as their exemplar by way of art, so evils, falling short of the art-form, fall short of the measure's rectitude; so Augustine defines evil as privation of mode (falling short of measure), species (of imitation of the exemplar), and order (of the end).
claims: Evil is privation of mode, species, and order.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e169.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Will has the complete character of cause, since its object is the end under the character of good, the cause of causes, and so it commands the other powers, which is why God's will is called absolutely the cause of things. Knowledge is not like will in this, nor does it relate to the known as life to the living.
claims: Will is the complete cause, as directed to the end.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e172.summary: The first sed contra is granted.
claims: God's knowledge does not cause evils.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e175.summary: Reply to the second sed contra. As creatures do not come from God by necessity of nature or natural power, neither by necessity of knowledge, but by freedom of will, in which causality is completed, so he did not create whenever he knew, but whenever he willed.
claims: Creation follows God's free will, not his knowledge as such.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e187.summary: First argument that God's knowledge is not uniform about things known. Knowledge of things otherwise than they are is false, and God's is most true, and things have different modes.
claims: Knowledge must match the mode of things.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e190.summary: Second argument. Knowing by essence and by likeness are different modes (Augustine), and God knows himself by essence and creatures by likenesses in him.
claims: Self-knowledge and knowledge of creatures differ in mode.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e193.summary: Third argument. God knows goods through themselves and evils through another, which is a different mode. (The cross-reference reads Dist. 16, apparently meaning Dist. 36.)
claims: Goods and evils are known differently.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e197.summary: Fourth argument. God knows things as he gave them being (Dionysius), and he created man and horse by different concepts (Augustine).
claims: Different concepts, different knowledge.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e200.summary: Sed contra. Dionysius says God knows material things immaterially, many things unitedly, and so on.
claims: God knows the many unitedly.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e203.summary: Second sed contra. The mode of knowledge follows chiefly the medium, whose diversity yields opinion or science about the same thing, and God knows all by one medium, his essence.
claims: One medium, one mode.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e206.summary: Thomas's determination. In any knowledge there is the mode of the thing known and the mode of the knower, and the mode of knowledge is the knower's, not the thing's (Boethius), as sense knows a thing with material conditions and intellect without them, because knowledge is as the known is in the knower, and whatever is in something is in it in that thing's mode (Liber de causis). Since the divine intellect has supreme unity, its knowledge of all is uniform, all things being one in it. So 'God knows all uniformly' is true if the adverb expresses the mode of the act of knowing, false if it expresses the mode of the object, since God knows not only the thing but its proper mode and that different modes belong to different things.
claims: God's knowledge is uniform in its act but knows the diverse modes of things.
Knowledge follows the mode of the knower.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e209.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'Knowledge of a thing otherwise than it is is false' is ambiguous: if 'otherwise' designates the mode of knowledge it is false, since knowledge of material things is immaterial; if the mode of the known it is true, and concludes only that.
claims: Knowledge differs in mode from things without falsity.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e212.summary: Reply to the second argument. The essence by which God knows himself is also the likeness by which he knows all creatures, so he knows himself and others by the same medium; unity is on the side of the knower, diversity on the side of the known, since God relates to that medium by identity and creatures by imitation.
claims: One medium: God by identity, creatures by imitation.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e216.summary: Reply to the third argument. God knows goods and evils by the same medium, his essence, but goods, imitating it, and evils, departing from it, relate to it differently.
claims: Goods and evils relate differently to one medium.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e219.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. There is one divine essence by which God gave being to all and knows all (Dionysius); the otherness of concepts comes from the diversity of respects, which follows the diversity of things.
claims: Diverse rationes are respects of one essence.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e231.summary: First argument that God's knowledge is not of enuntiables. God knows things by their ideas, and an idea is the likeness of an incomplex thing.
claims: Ideas are of incomplex things.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e234.summary: Second argument. When the intellect understands affirmation and negation there is composition (De anima 3), and the divine intellect has none.
claims: Judgement involves composition.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e237.summary: Third argument. Time is mixed with the operation of affirming and denying, so every enunciation signifies with time, and the divine intellect is wholly free of time.
claims: Enunciation involves time.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e241.summary: Fourth argument. The divine intellect admits no falsity, and falsity can enter the operation of affirming or denying but not that of grasping quiddity (De anima 3), so only the latter should be attributed to God.
claims: Judgement admits falsity.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e244.summary: Sed contra. Our knowledge is of enunciations as well as things, so if God's were not, it would be more imperfect than ours.
claims: God's knowledge cannot be poorer than ours.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e247.summary: Second sed contra. God knows whatever he foretells, and he foretold many enuntiables through the prophets, like 'a virgin shall conceive' (Isa. 7).
claims: Prophecy implies knowledge of propositions.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e250.summary: Thomas's determination. Avicenna's and Algazel's views seem to imply that God does not know enuntiables, especially about singulars, since they hold he knows singulars only universally, in their universal causes, so he knows this individual but not that it now exists and later does not, as one might know tomorrow's eclipse by its causes but not whether it is now occurring without seeing it. Since God knows particulars perfectly in all their individual conditions (Dist. 36), he knows not only things but enuntiables and complexes, yet by simple knowledge in his own mode. In a thing there are its quiddity and its being, and to these correspond two operations of intellect: formation, grasping quiddities, the understanding of indivisibles; and composition, grasping a thing's being by composing an affirmation, since the being of a composite of matter and form, from which our knowledge comes, consists in a composition of form with matter or accident with subject. In God there are his nature and his being, and as his nature is cause and exemplar of all natures, his being is cause and exemplar of all being. So as by knowing his essence he knows every thing, by knowing his being he knows the being of each thing, and so all enuntiables, which signify being, not by a different operation or composition but simply, since his being is not other than his essence or a consequent composite; and as he knows good and evil by the same, he knows affirmations and negations by the same.
claims: God knows enuntiables by simple knowledge of his being, the exemplar of all being.
The two operations of intellect correspond to quiddity and being; in God both are one.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e253.summary: Reply to the first argument. The artisan's form differs from the divine idea: it causes only the form of the artefact, so the artisan knows that this house exists and what follows its nature only through sense, but the divine idea causes all that is in the thing, so through it God knows not only the thing's nature but that it exists at such a time and all conditions following from matter or form.
claims: The divine idea causes the whole thing, including its existence at a time.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e256.summary: Reply to the second argument. Divine being, simple, is the exemplar of all composite being in creatures, so through it God knows without composition or division of concepts all being or non-being belonging to a thing; our intellect, knowing from things with composite being, grasps that being only by composing and dividing, and the Philosopher speaks of such an intellect.
claims: God knows composite being through his simple being.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e260.summary: Reply to the third argument. Time enters our composing and dividing for two reasons: on the side of our intellect, which takes knowledge from the continuum and time through sense and imagination, and on the side of what is understood, which is in time. In the divine intellect time enters only on the side of what is understood, since as he knows other things determinately he knows time, and so knows this thing to be at this or that time, but on the side of the intellect no time or succession enters, since he knows temporal things atemporally.
claims: God knows temporal things atemporally.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e263.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. As falsity enters our grasp of quiddities only incidentally, where knowledge of a composite quiddity depends on affirmation (Metaphysics 9), so falsity cannot enter the divine intellect either in grasping natures or enuntiables, since it knows both by the same operation and by one simple thing.
claims: God's one operation excludes falsity in both.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e276.summary: First argument that God's knowledge cannot be of non-beings. Knowledge implies relation to the knowable, and names relating God to creatures are said only when creatures exist (Lord, Creator).
claims: Relative names need existing creatures.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e279.summary: Second argument. Knowledge is only of truths (Posterior Analytics), and true and being are convertible.
claims: Knowledge is of beings.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e282.summary: Third argument. God's knowledge measures the known, and non-beings are commensurate with nothing.
claims: Non-beings are not measured.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e286.summary: Fourth argument. Being is the first object of intellect (Avicenna), and no power knows anything without its first object, as sight sees nothing without light.
claims: Being is the first object of intellect.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e289.summary: Sed contra. Whatever is chosen without error is known, and Augustine says things that are not are chosen, without error by God the chooser.
claims: God chooses non-existents knowingly.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e292.summary: Second sed contra. As the knowable is prior to our knowledge, God's knowledge is prior to the knowable, and there are knowables we do not know (the Philosopher), so God's knowledge can be of what does not exist.
claims: God's knowledge can exceed existents.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e295.summary: Thomas's determination. Whatever is known must in some way be, at least in the knower, as Avicenna says nothing can be stated of what is wholly non-being, so things relate to divine knowledge as they relate to being. A thing's being is threefold: in its own nature, drawn from its principles; in the potency of a cause; and in the apprehension of a knower. Everything that has being in its nature at any time God knew eternally, grasping its nature and seeing it to be, not only in his knowledge or in a cause's potency, but in its natural being, since when it exists he knows its being in its nature, and if from eternity he knew only its being in knowledge or cause his knowledge would advance with time; this is called knowledge of vision. Things that never have being in their own nature he knows as being in the potency of a cause, a defecting creature for evils or his operative power for goods, and as in his knowledge, as he knows that he knows them and can make them (goods) or that they can happen from creaturely defect (evils); this is called knowledge of simple understanding, since by it the simple nature of a thing that could be is known, but not its simple being, which is properly the object of vision, except in some respect.
claims: God knows all that ever exists by knowledge of vision, seeing it in its natural being.
He knows the merely possible by knowledge of simple understanding, as in a cause's power and in his knowledge.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e298.summary: Reply to the first argument. Relations founded on an actual operation going out to creatures can belong to God only from time, when creatures exist, but the relation implied in knowledge, power, and will is not founded on an operation actually going out to creatures, so the cases differ.
claims: Knowledge, power, and will are not temporal relations.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e301.summary: Reply to the second argument. God knows non-beings as they have truth: what will be in a thousand years he does not know to be now, since that is not true, but to be future then, when it will be true; what never is, was, or will be he knows to be in his knowledge and in the potency of its causes, as it is true that they are so.
claims: God knows things as they are truly.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e305.summary: Reply to the third argument. What does not exist is known by God not as actually commensurate with his knowledge but as commensurable, which suffices for truth.
claims: Non-beings are commensurable.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e308.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Whatever is known is known as being, in its own nature, in its cause, or in some knowledge, and so all God knows are beings.
claims: Everything known is known as some kind of being.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e320.summary: First argument that God's knowledge is not of contingents. It causes all goods known, and every necessary, unfailing cause produces necessary effects, so what it is of is necessary.
claims: A necessary cause yields necessary effects.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e323.summary: Second argument. Knowledge is only of truths, and in future contingents neither side is determinately true (the Philosopher).
claims: Future contingents lack determinate truth.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e326.summary: Third argument. Suppose God knows Socrates is running. Either it is possible he not run or not. If not, he necessarily runs. If so, posit it, since positing the possible yields nothing impossible; but God knows he runs, so God would know what is not, and his knowledge would be false. So his not running was not possible, and his running is necessary.
claims: Positing the possible opposite makes God's knowledge false.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e330.summary: Fourth argument, against necessity of consequence, not of the consequent. In every true conditional, if the antecedent is absolutely necessary, so is the consequent (Posterior Analytics 1). In 'if it is foreknown by God, Socrates runs' the antecedent is absolutely necessary, as past and as eternal, so the consequent is too.
claims: A necessary antecedent yields a necessary consequent.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e333.summary: Fifth argument. From a necessary major and assertoric minor follows a necessary conclusion (Prior Analytics): everything known by God is necessarily true; this is known by God; so it is necessarily true.
claims: Modal syllogism yields necessity.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e336.summary: Sixth argument, against distinguishing de dicto and de re. That distinction holds only for forms separable from the subject, not inseparable ones (no one distinguishes 'a white swan can be black'); being known by God always accompanies its subject, since what is once known by God cannot be unknown.
claims: De dicto/de re fails for inseparable predicates.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e339.summary: Seventh argument, against knowing contingents only as present or past. Knowledge of something present that was not had when it was future grows with time, and God's knowledge gains nothing from things and has no succession, so if he does not know future contingents as future he knows them in no way.
claims: God cannot gain knowledge over time.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e342.summary: Sed contra. What falls under free choice is maximally contingent, and God knows it, or he would not render to each according to his works.
claims: God knows free acts.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e345.summary: Second sed contra. God's knowledge is of all things, and not all things happen by necessity, as sense shows, philosophers prove, and faith presupposes.
claims: Not all things are necessary.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e349.summary: Thomas's determination. Because of such difficulties some philosophers denied God knowledge of particular contingents, conceiving the divine intellect like ours. That particularity from matter does not impede it was shown (Dist. 36); it remains whether contingency does. Contingency seems to escape divine knowledge in two ways: by the order of cause to effect, since a necessary, immutable cause seems to have necessary effects; and by the order of knowledge to known, since knowledge, being certain, requires certainty and determination in the known, which contingency excludes, even apart from causality, as in our knowledge and God's of evils. Neither removes God's knowledge of contingents. As to the first: where many causes are ordered, the last effect follows not the first cause but the proximate one in necessity or contingency, since the first cause's power is received in the second in its mode, as a tree's flowering has the sun's motion as remote and its generative power as proximate cause and can be impeded though the sun is invariable; so God's knowledge is the invariable cause of all, but through necessary secondary causes it produces necessary effects and through contingent ones contingent effects. The second is harder: a necessary first cause can coexist with a secondary cause's defect, but God's knowledge cannot coexist with it (God cannot know this man will run and he fail to run), by certainty, not causality, and certainty requires some certainty in the known. Before a thing exists it is only in its causes. Some causes necessarily produce their effect and cannot be impeded, and there the effect is certain and determined and can be demonstratively known (sunrise, eclipse); some produce it for the most part but fail sometimes, giving conjectural knowledge, more certain as the causes are more determined, like a doctor's prognosis or an astrologer's weather forecast; and some are open to either outcome, and there the future effect has no certainty or determination, so contingents ad utrumlibet cannot be known in their causes at all. But once realized they have determinate being in themselves and are known with certainty, as one who sees Socrates running, since Socrates' running while he runs is necessary. So the divine intellect beholds from eternity each contingent not only as in its causes but as in its determinate being. If he saw the thing in its determinate being only when it exists, he would know it differently after than before, and his knowledge would grow; so from eternity he saw not only his ordering to the thing but its very being. How this is Boethius shows (end of the Consolation): all knowledge is in the mode of the knower, and God is eternal, so his knowledge has the mode of eternity, wholly simultaneous without succession; as his eternity, one and indivisible like a standing now, is present to all times, his knowledge beholds all temporal things, though successive among themselves, as present to him, none future to him but one relative to another. So it is better called providence (pro-videre, seeing from afar) than prevision, seeing all as present at one glance from the watchtower of eternity, though it can be called foreknowledge of what is future to us, not to him. Example: five men seeing five contingent events in five successive hours each see theirs as present; if the five acts were one act, one knowledge would be present to all. Since God sees all times by one eternal, non-successive gaze, he sees all contingents at different times eternally as present, not only as in his knowledge but each time and the thing as being in this time and failing in that, and not only as future relative to an earlier time and past relative to a later, but the time in which it is present and the thing present in it, which cannot happen in our successive intellect. So nothing prevents God from having certain knowledge of contingents ad utrumlibet, since his gaze bears on the contingent as present in act, when its being is determined.
claims: The effect follows the proximate cause in necessity or contingency, so God's necessary knowledge can cause contingent effects through contingent causes.
God knows future contingents with certainty because his eternal knowledge sees each as present in its determinate being.
Divine knowledge is better called providence than prevision.
concepts: eternity as present to all times

ta-l1d38q1-d1e352.summary: Reply to the first argument. The effect takes necessity not from the first cause but only from the proximate cause, so the argument fails.
claims: Necessity comes from the proximate cause.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e355.summary: Reply to the second argument. A future contingent is not determinately true before it happens, lacking a determinate cause, so our intellect, knowing in a determinate time and successively, cannot know it with certainty; but while in act it is determinately true and can be known with certainty by a knowledge present to that act, as with bodily sight; and since divine knowledge is measured by eternity, which remaining the same is present to every time, it sees each contingent as in its act.
claims: God's eternal knowledge is present to each contingent in act.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e358.summary: Reply to the third argument. The act of divine knowledge bears on the contingent even if it is future now, as our sight bears on it while it is, and since what is, when it is, is necessary, though not absolutely, the contingent is contingent in itself but necessary as related to God's knowledge, to which it relates only as in actual being, as Socrates' running, which I see, is contingent in itself but necessary relative to my sight. So the distinction of necessity of consequence, not of consequent, or conditional, not absolute necessity, is good.
claims: Contingents are necessary relative to God's knowledge as what is, when it is, is necessary.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e361.summary: Reply to the fourth argument, surveying answers. Some say the antecedent 'this is foreknown by God' is not necessary, since past-tense statements depending on the future, like 'this was going to be', are not necessary; but though what was going to be may not come to be, it cannot not have been going to be, and 'foreknown' implies an act signified as past. Others, apparently Lombard, say it is not necessary because 'foreknown' co-signifies past time but signifies a divine act to which pastness does not belong, so as God can not foreknow he can not have foreknown; but immanent divine acts, though without necessity of coercion, have necessity of immobility, so the problem remains. Others say the antecedent is contingent, including an immutable divine act and a mutable order to the future; but the order to the future is the object of the act, a dictum taken materially, which makes no difference of necessity or contingency to the proposition, whose truth and necessity depend on the main verb ('I say Socrates runs' and 'I say the sun moves' are equally necessary). Others say the antecedent is necessary but the consequent not, the rule holding only where the antecedent is the proximate cause; but the Philosopher proves the rule from consequence, not causality. So Thomas says the antecedent is absolutely necessary, by the immobility of the act and by its order to the known, since the thing falls under divine knowledge only while in act, when it is determined and certain, for what is necessarily is while it is. So a similar necessity must be placed in the consequent, taking 'Socrates runs' as in act, determined and necessary; taken as following from the antecedent, it is necessary, since it follows only as subject to divine knowledge, which regards it as present in actual being: it is necessary that Socrates run while he runs.
claims: The antecedent 'foreknown by God' is absolutely necessary, and the consequent is necessary as present in act, not absolutely.
Earlier solutions (past-future statements, divine act timeless, mixed antecedent, causal reading of the rule) fail.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e364.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. 'Everything known by God is necessary' is ambiguous de dicto (true) and de re (false), and so is the conclusion. The thing can be taken under the condition by which it falls under divine knowledge, as having determinate being in act, and so it is necessary; or without condition, and so not necessary, since it can be considered as in its causes before it is in act, where it has no necessity and is not known by God as future-determined, since God does not know a contingent effect to be determined in its cause, which would be false knowledge.
claims: De dicto the proposition is true, de re false.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e368.summary: Reply to the sixth argument. Though this respect to the thing is inseparable as it attains it, it attains it only as considered present in actual being, so the distinction holds as the thing is considered as falling under that respect or not. Socrates' running falls under the certainty of divine knowledge as in act, which it did not always have, since it was once only potential and as such not subject to that certainty; if God saw the cause, Socrates, and not immediately the effect in its being, as we know the future, he could never know it. So the de re/de dicto distinction is good.
claims: The thing falls under God's certain knowledge only as actual, so the distinction applies.
concepts: de dicto vs. de re upheld

ta-l1d38q1-d1e371.summary: Reply to the seventh argument. God knows not only what is present to us but what is past and future to us, on all of which the divine gaze falls as present in their times, so it does not follow that God sometimes knows something he once did not.
claims: God's knowledge does not grow over time.

ta-l1d38q1-d1e380.summary: An expositio textus. 'Because it is future, it is known by God' denotes the cause of the consequence, not of being. 'He foreknew their sins, not his own' means that if his foreknowledge compelled them to sin, they would not sin, acting under compulsion, but God would be the compeller.
claims: Foreknowledge does not cause sin.

ta-l1d38q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 38 divides Lombard's treatment of God's knowledge in relation to the known, its causality and ineffability, and announces five articles: causality, uniformity, enuntiables, non-beings, and contingents.
claims: Future things do not cause foreknowledge.

ta-l1d38q1-Dd1e120.summary: Article 1 holds that God's knowledge causes things as an artisan's art does, showing end and form, but complete causality requires will, so it is the knowledge of approval that causes things and creation follows God's free will. It does not cause evils, which deviate from form and end and are privations of mode, species, and order.
claims: God's knowledge causes goods as art joined with will; it does not cause evils.

ta-l1d38q1-Dd1e179.summary: Article 2 holds that God's knowledge is uniform in its act, since knowledge follows the mode of the knower, but knows the diverse modes of things. One medium, his essence, relates to God by identity and to creatures by imitation, and to goods and evils differently.
claims: God's knowledge is uniform in act, diverse in object.

ta-l1d38q1-Dd1e223.summary: Article 3 holds, against implications of Avicenna and Algazel, that God knows enuntiables. As he knows all natures through his essence, he knows the being of each thing through his being, the exemplar of all being, by one simple act without composition, time, or falsity, knowing each thing's existence at its time.
claims: God knows enuntiables simply, through his being.

ta-l1d38q1-Dd1e268.summary: Article 4 holds that God knows non-beings. What ever exists he knows by knowledge of vision, seeing it in its natural being. What never exists he knows by knowledge of simple understanding, as in a cause's potency and in his knowledge. Knowledge, power, and will are not temporal relations, and non-beings are known as commensurable and as true in their way.
claims: God knows actuals by vision and possibles by simple understanding.

ta-l1d38q1-Dd1e312.summary: Article 5 holds that God knows contingents with certainty. Effects follow their proximate causes in necessity or contingency, so God's immutable knowledge produces contingent effects through contingent causes. Future contingents, undetermined in their causes, are determined in their actual being, and God's eternal knowledge, present to all times at once (Boethius), sees each as present in act. Contingents are necessary relative to God's knowledge only as what is, when it is, is necessary. The antecedent 'foreknown by God' is necessary and the consequent necessary only as present, and the de dicto/de re distinction holds.
claims: God knows future contingents certainly because eternity is present to all times.
Contingency is preserved by proximate causes and by conditional necessity.

ta-l1d38q1-Dd1e375.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 38 explains that 'because it is future it is known' gives the cause of consequence, not of being, and that God's foreknowledge does not compel sins.
claims: Foreknowledge does not cause sin.

ta-l1d38q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 38 treats God's knowledge in relation to things known. Article 1 holds that it causes goods as art joined with will, not evils. Article 2 holds that it is uniform in act while knowing the diverse modes of things. Article 3 holds that God knows enuntiables simply through his being. Article 4 distinguishes knowledge of vision of actuals from knowledge of simple understanding of possibles. Article 5 holds that God knows contingents with certainty, since effects follow proximate causes in contingency and his eternal knowledge sees all times as present, contingents being necessary only conditionally.
claims: God's knowledge causes goods with will, knows enuntiables and possibles, and knows future contingents certainly.
Eternity's presence to all times reconciles foreknowledge with contingency.
